title: All will forget
hook: soon you'll forget everything, and soon everything will forget you (Meditations 7.21)

segments.voice: Yesterday: emerald, which stays green whatever anyone does. Your line was keep my color. Did you stay in your own shade? Day five hundred eighty-nine.

Try naming all eight of your great-grandparents. It's harder than it sounds. Maybe one name comes, maybe a story about a farm or a ship. These were people with whole lives: first loves, embarrassments, opinions about the neighbors, worries about what people thought of them. Every one of those worries is gone now, and so are most of the people who could have remembered them. That can sound bleak. Marcus Aurelius treated it as a kind of relief, and he wrote it down in one short line.
screen: `YOUR GREAT-GRANDPARENTS.` → `WORRIES, ALL GONE.` → `A KIND OF RELIEF.`

segments.voice: First, the line. Meditations seven, twenty-one, in George Long's translation, is just this: "Near is thy forgetfulness of all things; and near the forgetfulness of thee by all." Two forgettings, facing each other. Soon you'll forget everything. Soon everything will forget you. Second, who wrote it. This is an emperor, a man whose face was stamped on coins. If anyone could hope to be remembered, it was Marcus. And we do still know his name. But the opinions of the people around him, the senators, the courtiers, the crowd, on any given Tuesday? Those are gone. Third, what it's for. Marcus uses this line as medicine for one particular sickness: worry about reputation. He comes back to it again and again in the Meditations. What will they think. What will they say about me. Marcus's answer is not that people's opinions don't exist. It's that they're brief. The ones who praise you will be forgotten, and so will the ones who mock you. A worry built on something that short shouldn't get to run your whole day. Fourth, the freedom in it. On Marcus's view, if embarrassments are soon forgotten, much of the fear around them has nothing to stand on. The awkward thing you said in the meeting. The post that didn't land. The question you were afraid to ask. They'll vanish, like your great-grandparents' worries. What's left is whether you did good while you were here.
screen: `TWO FORGETTINGS, FACE TO FACE.` · `EVEN THE EMPEROR'S CROWD.` · `MEDICINE FOR REPUTATION WORRY.` · `WHAT'S LEFT: THE GOOD YOU DID.` · then, large: `ALL WILL FORGET.`

segments.voice: Sit, and breathe. Bring up one worry about how you look to others. A mistake at work, something you said, a photo, a fear of seeming foolish. Hold it plainly. Now look ahead, long after you're gone. Nobody alive remembers it. Not one person. Let the worry sit in that long quiet. Notice what's left when it shrinks. Then let it go, on an out-breath. The bell holds the time.
Marcus, who wrote that you'll soon forget everything, and everything will soon forget you, as medicine for worrying what people think. Today's word.
Your line: two forgettings facing each other. The next time you catch yourself worrying how something will look, say the line, and do the honest thing anyway. Day five hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus often use 7.21 when anxious about reputation, reminding themselves that both praise and embarrassment are soon forgotten, and turning back to what they can do well now.

original.note: Greek: forgetting. In myth, Lethe was the river of forgetfulness in the underworld.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gloomy line about death.
what it means: both praise and embarrassment are brief, so worry about reputation shouldn't run your life.
what a scholar hears: the forgetting of fame comes back again and again in the Meditations (4.19 and 4.33, for example); 7.21 states it in its barest form.
recall: the ruling part, the steering center

notes: Editor review (y2 pass): fixed a count error (everyone has eight great-grandparents, not four); cut 'most people can't', the 'most comforting fact' superlative, 'every coin' and 'three continents', 'once you really believe' (telling the listener what they believe), the 'hundred years' number, and the 'most frequent themes' superlative.

The coin and statue claims are general (Marcus's portraits appeared on imperial coinage and statues throughout the empire); 'three continents' refers to Europe, Asia and Africa within the empire. Confirm framing.
Fame's forgetting as a frequent theme: e.g. 4.19, 4.33, 8.21. Confirm references.
Lethe as the river of forgetfulness: standard mythology.
